newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: LUXEMBOURG'S SES SEES NO STOCK FLOTATION FOR NOW.
newsitem.headline: LUXEMBOURG'S SES SEES NO STOCK FLOTATION FOR NOW.

text.p: Luxembourg-based Societe Europeenne des Satellites (SES), which runs the Astra satellite network, said on Thursday it did not see an immediate need for an IPO, though one was possible in the future.

"We have no specific plans and no timetable for an IPO (initial public offering)," SES spokesman Yves Feltes told Reuters. "The financing of the four satellites under construction is secured so there is no need for an IPO."

Deutsche Bank Luxembourg, which helped found SES and is a subsidiary of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, said in April it might offer part of its 4.24 percent in SES in a listing operation which it hoped could take place in the "not too distant future".
SES was set up 12 years ago as a high-risk venture under a franchise agreement granted by the Grand Duchy, as only a sovereign state can apply for satellite positions in space.

As a result, 20 percent of SES's shares are B shares, equally divided between the Luxembourg state's Banque et Caisse d'Epargne de l'Etat (BCEE) and Societe Nationale de Credit et d'Investissement (SNCI). The participations give them together a third of the total votes on SES's board of directors.
"They have a blocking minority. They are less interested in a flotation than the private shareholders and would want to see their special status preserved," Feltes added.
In 1996 SES paid 2.1 billion francs in taxes and franchise fees, making it a major contributer to government revenue.
SES sales rose 37 percent to 14.1 billion francs, while net profit soared 67 percent to 4.8 billion. Revenue comes mostly from leasing the transponders on its satellites to broadcasters.
In the same year SES invested 13.3 billion francs in additional satellites and ground equipment.
